questions.q: What does NULL mean in Tableau?
options: No value at all — genuinely missing data, distinct from zero or an empty string
The number zero
An empty text string
A deleted row that Tableau still counts
questions.explain: NULL means the data is genuinely missing — not zero, not blank text — which is exactly why arithmetic on a NULL can quietly break a calculation.

options: Returns Discount's real value if it isn't NULL, or 0 if it is
Returns TRUE if Discount is NULL, FALSE otherwise
Always returns 0, regardless of Discount's value
Deletes any row where Discount is NULL
questions.explain: IFNULL(expression, fallback) passes the expression through unchanged if it's not NULL, and substitutes the fallback value if it is.

questions.q: What is ZN([Sales]) functionally equivalent to?
options: IFNULL([Sales], 0)
ISNULL([Sales])
STR([Sales])
DATE([Sales])
questions.explain: ZN is shorthand specifically for converting a NULL numeric value to 0 — functionally the same as IFNULL([Sales], 0), just shorter and numeric-specific.

questions.q: Which function would you use to convert a text field like "2024-07-17" into a real Tableau date?
options: DATE(expr)
STR(expr)
INT(expr)
ISNULL(expr)
questions.explain: DATE(expr) converts a value — including a text string in a recognizable date format — into a real date Tableau can use in date functions and timelines.

questions.q: When a calculation fails to save with an error like "expects a [type] argument," what is almost always the fix?
options: Wrap one side of the mismatched expression in the right conversion function (STR, INT, FLOAT, or DATE)
Delete the calculated field and start over from scratch
Add ISNULL around the entire formula
Rename the calculated field to something shorter
questions.explain: Tableau is strict about mixing types in one expression — the fix is almost always converting one side to match the other's type before the operator that's complaining.
